subject: Detecting aberrant responses using person fit statistics

messages.author: 9403604069d4685f
messages.subject: Detecting aberrant responses using person fit statistics
parts:
Dear Phil,

I've been reading a paper (DOI: 10.3102/1076998618825116) where authors propose an iterative procedure to detect aberrant responses in a sample of test takers. Just to summarize the important points, this is what the procedure looks like:

1. Estimate item parameters on the full sample
2. Flag participants whose person-fit statistic is below the cutoff
3. Estimate item parameters on the reduced sample (without flagged participants). Use those item parameters from the REDUCED sample to compute person parameters from the FULL sample
4. Repeat 2 & 3 until the difference in the percentage of flagged participant in the current and previous iteration is less than 0.01

Now, my question: the authors in the linked paper use a lz* statistic of person fit. I am wondering do you think it would be possible to use the Zh statistic from your package to follow the same procedure? Are you aware of any theoretical and/or mathematical reasons that would prevent this usage? As far as I know, the lz* statistic is used only for binary items and I am interested in detecting aberrant responses on Likert scales.

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Detecting aberrant responses using person fit statistics
parts:
I also am not aware of the polytomous generalization to this statistic, though it could very well be that nobody has generalized it yet. The PerFit package contains a number of these person-fit type indices, so you might have some luck there.

Regarding the paper, the approach these authors took is a pretty aggressive one, and reminds me a lot of fitting regression models after iteratively removing all cases that have even minimally large residuals. An alternative strategy, which doesn't require the standardized lz* versions of the statistic, is to apply a weight function to each response vector according to these person fit measures. 

E.g., compute the original model, obtain Zh for each case (or lz*), and obtain the weight w = 1/abs(Zh). Given this weight vector, pass the result to the survey.weight input to re-estimate the model to obtain a model that is less influenced by the originally contaminated observations. Under this approach, cases that are initially deemed unusual get progressively less weight in the final model. You could obviously repeat this process if you wanted to, but in the end it has the same effect (and in the limiting case where the w -> 0 in really unusual cases then this is equivalent to removing the observations entirely. Hence, the data removal approach is a limiting subset of this weighted approach). HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Detecting aberrant responses using person fit statistics

Was just looking through previous discussions to see if there was anything on what mirt does when computing person fit, and whether it has the lz* generalization to polytomous items. Came across this thread. I think generalizations of lz* do exist, but I don't (yet) see an R package that can do them:
http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/s11336-015-9465-x
